object.description: A column of solid wrought iron 7.21 metres tall, 41 centimetres across and over six tonnes in weight, standing in the courtyard of the Qutb complex in Delhi. A Sanskrit inscription in Gupta script says it was raised as a standard of Vishnu by a king called Chandra, almost certainly Chandragupta II, who reigned from about 375 to 415 CE; it was probably first set up at Udayagiri in central India and moved to Delhi in the eleventh century, two hundred years before the Qutb Minar was built beside it. No one else in the world could make a single iron object this large for another thousand years: it was built up by forge-welding many lumps of hot iron, hammered together by hand. Most famously, it has stood in the open for sixteen centuries without rusting. The reason is the metal itself: a high phosphorus content, a product of the ancient Indian smelting process, lets a thin protective film of iron hydrogen phosphate form on the surface and seal it. Scientists did not understand this until the 1990s.
facts: 7.21 m tall including 1.12 m below ground; 41 cm in diameter at the base; estimated weight over six tonnes.
The oldest inscription names King Chandra and dedicates the pillar to Vishnu; it covers about 65 by 27 cm of the surface.
Its rust resistance comes from phosphorus in the iron, which forms a protective crystalline layer (misawite).
Moved to Delhi by the Tomar king Anangpal II in the 11th century, long before the mosque now around it.
